Mr. Vice President, We are living in an era of rapidly evolving and emerging technologies and pervasive digitalization, which has serious implications for human rights. Advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning, surveillance technologies, commercial satellite services, cloud infrastructure, autonomous platforms, predictive analytics, and digital financing are transforming the way that actors under our mandate operate. Through technology, actors under our mandate are increasingly undertaking functions once the exclusive preserve of states, often with limited transparency, accountability, oversight and monitoring, with profound adverse impacts on human rights. The report argues that technology-enabled mercenarism, which is the development, sale, deployment and provision of for-profit offensive and defensive cyber, digital, geospatial and autonomous tools, by private actors, such as actors under our mandate, for or on behalf of state and non-state clients enable espionage, surveillance, disruption, attack, sabotage, warfare, and information operations across online accounts and platforms, networks, devices, and other infrastructures. This technologization of private force can occur in the context of armed hostilities, concerted acts of violence, undermining the constitutional order and territorial integrity of states, as well as undermining the rights of peoples to self-determination. As conflicts proliferate, states are relying more on private military and security companies and technology companies to collect, store, process, and analyze battlefield data. Actors under our mandate are increasingly involved in operating uncrewed aerial systems inclusive of drones, quadcopters, and counter uncrewed aerial systems, geospatial intelligence systems, signals intelligence, synthetic aperture radar technologies, as well as artificial intelligence-assisted targeting technologies. When machine-generated analysis and predictive systems are used to identify targets, often with limited human control or oversight, the risks of error, bias, and misidentification become significant. The right to life is therefore directly implicated. Surveillance technologies, facial recognition systems, biometric databases, and artificial intelligence enabled monitoring tools are being widely developed and used by private actors, inclusive of actors under our mandate against human rights defenders, activists, journalists, students, indigenous peoples, and minority communities. Information gathered through technological systems in some cases has been used to facilitate arbitrary arrest and detention, restrict and curtail freedom of movement, intimidate and silence local populations, and engage in lethal kinetic operations. Advanced technology designed, developed, and deployed by private actors has a disproportionate impact on vulnerable people, including Indigenous peoples, women, children, people with disabilities, ethnic and religious minorities, and human rights defenders. Of notable concern is the use of synthetic AI-generated content broadcast across digital and social media platforms to recruit children and young people into armed hostilities and spread hate, violence, and disinformation. Mr. Vice President, while technological capabilities have evolved rapidly, accountability mechanisms have not kept apace. Victims often encounter immense difficulties in identifying those responsible for violations, accessing evidence, or obtaining justice.
